mainEntity.name: How often should I have my dental implants professionally checked?

acceptedAnswer.text: The frequency of professional maintenance visits varies depending on individual clinical factors. Many patients with implants attend a minimum of twice yearly, though some may benefit from more frequent monitoring, particularly in the early years following placement or if there are identified risk factors such as a history of gum disease. Your dental team will recommend a schedule appropriate to your specific needs following a clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can dental implants fail even with good oral hygiene?

acceptedAnswer.text: While excellent oral hygiene significantly reduces the risk of implant complications, it does not entirely eliminate all possibility of difficulty. Factors such as systemic health conditions, certain medications, bone quality, and occlusal forces can also influence outcomes. This is why professional monitoring is important even for patients who maintain very good home care. Treatment suitability and outcomes always depend on individual clinical circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Is it normal for the gum around an implant to bleed slightly when cleaning?

acceptedAnswer.text: Occasional, very minor bleeding during cleaning in the immediate post-placement period may occur, but persistent or recurring bleeding around an established implant is worth discussing with your dental team. It can be an early indicator of peri-implant mucositis, which is generally manageable when identified promptly. This is not a cause for alarm, but it is a useful signal to arrange a professional review sooner rather than later.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Peri-implant mucositis involves inflammation of the soft tissue (gum) around the implant without associated bone loss. It is considered reversible with appropriate professional treatment and improved home care. Peri-implantitis is a more advanced condition involving both soft tissue inflammation and progressive loss of the supporting bone around the implant. It requires more involved clinical management and, if left unaddressed, can threaten the stability of the implant.

mainEntity.name: Can I use a water flosser instead of regular floss for my implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Water flossers — also known as oral irrigators — can be a valuable addition to your implant cleaning routine, particularly for implant-supported bridges or where access with conventional floss is limited. However, they are generally considered a complement to mechanical cleaning rather than a complete substitute. Your dental team can advise on the most effective interdental cleaning approach for your specific implant restoration.

mainEntity.name: Do implants require any special cleaning products?

acceptedAnswer.text: Generally, a soft-bristled toothbrush and non-abrasive fluoride toothpaste are suitable for daily cleaning around implants. Specialist implant cleaning aids such as implant-specific interdental brushes or floss are available and may be recommended depending on your restoration type. It is advisable to seek guidance from your dental team on specific product recommendations, as the most appropriate tools will depend on the design and location of your particular implant restoration.
